newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Summit reveals insecurity as 21st century looms.
newsitem.headline: Summit reveals insecurity as 21st century looms.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

Europe is about to leave behind a century of bloody confrontation but a security summit that ended on Tuesday provided little reassurance for many that the new millennium will bring lasting peace and stability.

More than 50 leaders from Europe, the United States and Canada issued a series of worthy declarations intended to reassure everyone that the age of conflict and Cold War tension has been replaced by the warm glow of cooperation.

"We...believe that history has offered us an unprecedented opportunity. Freedom, democracy and cooperation among our nations and peoples are now the foundation for our common security," the leaders said in their final declaration.

What the summit actually showed was the degree of insecurity still felt by many, particularly Russia and other former Soviet republics, and the extent to which naked power and the pursuit of national interests still dominate relations between states.

Russia returned to the attack over NATO expansion, while Belarus and its Western critics argued about the development of democracy. Azerbaijan and Armenia remained stubbornly at odds over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.

One year after the end of the conflict in Bosnia, Europe's worst war in half a century, the message from the two-day Lisbon summit was not entirely gloomy -- democracy is taking firmer root on the continent than at any time this century.

Bitter arguments over how to deal with the conflict in former Yugoslavia, which helped wreck the last summit held by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in 1994, have now subsided.
The peace deal in Bosnia has given a new lease of life to NATO and the 54-nation OSCE, and helped define the roles of such organisations better than any grand scheme on paper.
The summit agreed to start a new round of arms talks that will help bring stability to the continent by limiting military hardware from the Atlantic to the Urals.
But the Lisbon meeting was, equally, a vivid illustration that unresolved ethnic conflicts and regional tensions still plague Europe's attempts to find real peace.
It also ran into problems every time it tried to deal with one central question that preoccupies many countries.
How can all nations enjoy equal security and respect, as the summit promised, when only some are members of powerful Western institutions like NATO and the European Union?
Russia played on this theme particularly strongly, arguing that plans for NATO expansion would leave it isolated.
"Is it not clear that the appearance of new dividing lines would lead to a worsening of the whole geopolitical situation in the world?," asked Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
Western leaders like U.S. Vice President Al Gore and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl stuck to their claim that NATO expansion would provide more security for all, not create new divisions.

Nevertheless, the difference will be clear. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic will have cast-iron guarantees of Western military assistance if they join NATO as expected. Nobody else outside NATO will be able to count on that support.

As an alternative, Russia proposed strengthening the OSCE since it is a leading member of the forum. Almost all other countries opposed the idea, suspicious that Moscow might then try and use the organisation to exercise veto power over NATO.
The fact that such suspicions still exist, seven years after the Berlin Wall fell, shows that two world wars and a Cold War have left deep scars which are unlikely to heal soon.
Kohl touched on these continued insecurities when he told fellow leaders at the summit that Europe was now standing at a "great crossroads".

"We Europeans will see whether we are capable of taking this chance for a future of peace and freedom," he said, "or whether 'Euroscepticism' and withdrawal into national isolation will win the upper hand -- so that we miss the chance of the century."
